newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan firm could soon begin China shipping route.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan firm could soon begin China shipping route.

text.p: Taiwan's Uniglory Marine Corp has obtained initial approval from Chinese port authorities to become the first shipping firm to legally sail directly between Taiwan and China, a newspaper said on Sunday.

The firm's application to sail across the Taiwan Strait between Taiwan's southern Kaohsiung port and mainland China's southeastern port city of Xiamen has been approved by local port authorities in Xiamen, the Liberty Times said.
It could begin the route as early as mid-March after first obtaining further approval from Beijing authorities, the paper said.
Uniglory plans to use its Panama-registered ship, Li Shun, on the weekly crossing, it said.
Company officials were not available for comment on Sunday.

Taiwanese and Chinese negotiators reached an understanding on January 22 in unofficial talks in Hong Kong that could end Taipei's decades-old ban on direct shipping between the island and Chinese mainland.
Non-government negotiators said they agreed to allow authorised shipping companies to seek approval from China to sail directly between Kaohsiung and China's ports of Fuzhou and Xiamen.
Kaohsiung is Taiwan's main southern port. It lies 300 km (185 miles) east of Fuzhou and Xiamen.

To fulfil its ambition of becoming an Asia-Pacific business hub, Taiwan proposed in 1995 setting up an offshore transshipment centre at Kaohsiung port from which ships would be allowed to sail directly between Taiwan and China.
The project has been delayed by sovereignty issues.

On August 20, 1996, China unveiled rules governing direct shipping links across the Taiwan Strait, effective immediately, but Taiwan responded coolly, saying Beijing's rules were "mingled with sensitive political issues".
Taiwan has banned direct air and shipping links with China since Chiang Kai-shek's Nationalists lost a civil war to the Chinese Communists and fled to the island in 1949.

With tensions easing since the late 1980s, civilian aircraft and vessels have skirted the ban by stopping over in a third country or territory such as the British colony of Hong Kong or the Portuguese-administered territory of Macau.
Taiwanese businesses, which have poured more than $20 billion into China, have pressured Taipei to establish direct shipping links to save transportation costs.
